summary: For ages 12–14, learners distinguish renewable from non-renewable energy resources and, crucially, evaluate trade-offs between cost, reliability/intermittency and environmental impact. The cognitive heart is multi-criteria comparison and evidence-based argument, not memorising a list. Two independent axes must be kept apart: renewable↔non-renewable (will it run out?) and low-carbon↔high-carbon (climate impact), so nuclear (non-renewable, low-carbon) and biomass (renewable, emits CO2) occupy surprising quadrants. Reliability/intermittency is a further, separate consideration. Two core activities carry the objective: an energy-mix decision task where learners build a supply to meet demand and experience the consequences, and a written evidence-to-claim justification — because the NGSS practice is to construct an explanation/argument from evidence, this written task should not be reduced to recognition. Supporting activities cover classification/two-axis sorting, resource life-stories and a stakeholder debate.
misconceptions: 'Renewable = clean / no environmental impact' — biomass emits CO2, hydro floods habitats, wind/solar have manufacturing and land footprints; renewable refers to replenishment, not zero impact.
'Nuclear is renewable' (or 'renewable because low-carbon') — nuclear fuel is finite, so non-renewable, though low-carbon; the two axes are independent.
'Renewables never run out and are always available' — ignores intermittency/reliability (no wind on a calm day, no solar at night).
Confusing renewable with recyclable, or treating electricity itself as an energy 'source' rather than a carrier generated from a resource.
Mis-timing depletion ('fossil fuels will run out next year' or 'never') and conflating an energy RESOURCE with an energy STORE.

activities.title: Power the country: build an energy mix
steps: Given a demand curve across a day (and, if possible, across seasons), set the share of each resource — solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass, coal, oil, gas, nuclear — to meet demand.
Observe live readouts recomputing for cost, CO2 and reliability as you change the mix; a grid where supply falls below demand during low wind/sun suffers a blackout.
Test deliberate extremes: an all-wind grid on a calm evening, an all-coal grid (cheap but high CO2), and a nuclear-heavy grid (steady low-carbon baseload but costly and finite fuel).
Trigger events such as a calm day or a peak-demand evening to expose intermittency versus baseload.
Write a short justification for your chosen mix, citing the cost, CO2 and reliability evidence you observed.
activities.insight: There is no single 'best' resource — every choice trades reliability against cost against carbon, so meeting demand needs a MIX. 'Renewable' (won't run out) is a different axis from 'low-carbon' (climate): a renewable biomass plant still emits CO2 when it burns fuel, while a non-renewable nuclear plant emits no CO2 from generation itself and has low emissions over its whole life cycle.

activities.title: Write and defend an energy decision
steps: Given a data set on two or more resources (cost, CO2, reliability/intermittency, other environmental impacts such as land use or habitat), write a claim about which mix or resource a country should favour for a stated context.
Support the claim with specific evidence from the data and name at least one trade-off you are accepting.
State explicitly where science ends and values begin — which parts are measurable consequences and which are societal choices.
Revise your argument after reading a counter-position that weights the criteria differently.
activities.insight: Science describes consequences (CO2, depletion, land use, reliability) but society makes the choices; a strong answer reasons from evidence about criteria rather than reciting a slogan or a list.

activities.title: Classify on two axes and sort the surprising cases
steps: Sort each resource (solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, biomass; coal, oil, gas, nuclear) as renewable or non-renewable using the test: is it replenished on a human timescale?
Place the same resources on a second axis, low-carbon↔high-carbon, forming a two-axis grid.

Explain why nuclear lands in the non-renewable/low-carbon quadrant, and discuss where biomass belongs on the carbon axis: it is renewable if regrown, but it releases CO2 when burned, and its net carbon impact depends on how quickly the plants regrow and on emissions from harvesting and transport.
Match each resource to its characteristic impact (coal → CO2; hydro → flooded valleys/habitat loss; wind → manufacturing footprint + intermittency; nuclear → low-carbon but waste and finite fuel).
activities.insight: Renewable means replenished on a human timescale, not 'clean'; carbon intensity is a separate property. The two-axis sort forces the surprising cases (nuclear, biomass) into view.

activities.title: Resource life-stories reference
steps: Explore each resource in turn to reveal: the renewable test applied to it, where its energy originally comes from, its cost, its CO2, and its wider environmental impacts.
Trace the energy backwards (e.g. wind and coal both ultimately from the Sun) and decide whether that origin changes the renewable classification.
Use a two-axis overlay (renewable×carbon) to see where each resource sits.
activities.insight: Each resource has a distinct 'story' of origin, benefits and impacts; renewability is about the rate of replenishment of the primary source, not the ultimate origin of the energy.

activities.title: Interview the stakeholders
steps: Interview or challenge several in-role stakeholders — e.g. a wind-farm engineer, a climate scientist and an energy-policy maker — each of whom weights cost, reliability and environmental impact differently.
Press each on the downside of their preferred option and the merit of an option they dislike.
After hearing the positions, state your own reasoned judgement and name the trade-off you are accepting.
activities.insight: Because the topic has a genuine values dimension, different informed people reach different conclusions from the same evidence by weighting criteria differently; a defensible view must acknowledge trade-offs.

checkQuestion: A friend says: 'Electricity is a renewable energy source, because we can always make more of it.' Is electricity itself a renewable energy resource? Explain what actually makes an energy resource renewable or non-renewable.
checkAnswer: No — electricity isn't a renewable resource; it's a carrier of energy that we generate from a primary source. Whether it counts as 'renewable' depends on that source. A resource is renewable if it's naturally replenished on a human timescale (sunlight, wind, flowing water, geothermal heat, biomass); it's non-renewable if it exists as a finite stock that isn't meaningfully replaced — coal, oil, gas, and nuclear fuel.
